c0014: ▸ The first section of "Opening" covers personal hygiene and a safe start: exhaust fan first and, if you have gas for waffles or crepes, a gas-smell check before turning anything on.
c0015: ▸ A shop runs three different temperatures; never mix them up: storage 0 °F or below, dipping cabinet service 6–10 °F (per the manufacturer) and mix aging 36–39 °F, never above 41 °F. Dipping cabinets are NOT turned off at night: they stay on — on their night/storage setting if your model has one, per the manufacturer.
c0016: ▸ Allergens travel on the scoop: use the dipper well or one scoop per flavor. Water does not remove allergens: for an allergy order, wash hands, wear fresh gloves and use a clean, sanitized scoop. Cones, wafers and cookies contain wheat; pistachio, hazelnut and almond are tree nuts, and peanut butter flavors and toppings carry peanuts (US: 9 major allergens; UK: 14).
c0028: Clean uniform and apron, hair covered with a cap or hairnet, non-slip shoes
c0030: No jewelry on hands or arms except a plain band; short, clean, unpolished nails; no bare-hand contact with cones or toppings

c0036: If the production room or waffle/crepe area has GAS: check there is NO gas smell BEFORE lighting anything. If you smell gas, touch nothing, get everyone out and call the gas company or 911 from outside

c0103: ▸ Checklist for the two key production phases of artisan ice cream.
c0104: ▸ Pasteurizing: mix, heat treatment, cooling and aging. Note: pasteurizing your own mix usually requires a STATE frozen dessert or dairy manufacturer license (e.g. Vermont, Georgia; Arizona exempts on-premises sales with an approved plan), and some states also require one to batch-freeze pasteurized mix or run a soft serve machine (Vermont, Massachusetts); with bought pasteurized mix a health permit is usually enough. Check with your state department of agriculture or health.
c0105: ▸ Batch freezing: texturizing, draw, hardening and storage.
c0106: ▸ Adjust temperatures and times to your equipment and recipes.
c0107: ▸ Use the notes to log batches, yield and overrun.
c0108: ▸ Print and keep it in the production room next to the recipe cards.
c0110: ▸ At the bottom of "Batch Freezing" there is an editable shelf life table by food group: adjust it to your product and supplier. It sits outside the counter because it is a reference, not a task.
c0111: ▸ Pasteurized base mix is NOT frozen: it is aged at 36–39 °F (never above 41 °F) and batch-frozen within 3–5 days (kit criterion, inside the 7-day FDA date marking, 3-501.17). What gets frozen is the finished ice cream, at 0 °F or below.
c0114: Weigh all ingredients per the flavor recipe card
c0115: Blend dry ingredients (sugars, stabilizers, milk powder)
c0116: Add liquids (milk, cream) to the pasteurizer
c0118: Add the dry blend to the liquids with the mixer / high-shear blender
c0120: Add fats and emulsifiers (cream, butter, egg yolks, stabilizer blend) while the mix HEATS through 104–122 °F, before the pasteurizing hold: anything added after pasteurizing goes in raw — log reading: ____ °F
c0121: Pasteurize at 185 °F for 15 seconds (the kit's high-temp target); typical state minimums: batch 155 °F for 30 min or HTST 175 °F for 25 s — check your state rules and your pasteurizer's validated program, and keep the recording chart if your license requires one — log reading: ____ °F
c0122: Cool the mix fast to 41 °F or below: 135 → 70 °F within 2 h, then to 41 °F within 4 h (pasteurizer cooling cycle, a blast chiller or an ice bath; faster if your license says so) — log reading: ____ °F
c0123: Verify the final mix temperature (41 °F or below, ideally 36–39 °F) — log reading: ____ °F
c0124: Transfer the mix to a clean aging container
c0125: Label: flavor, date, aging start time, batch
c0126: Respect the aging time: minimum 4 h, ideal 8–12 h at 36–39 °F — log reading: ____ °F
c0127: Clean, then sanitize the pasteurizer after each use, per the manufacturer (test strip)
c0128: Record the production batch on the traceability sheet
c0131: Check that the mix has completed its aging time
c0132: Stir the mix gently before pouring it into the batch freezer
c0133: Set the batch freezer draw temperature (per the manufacturer): ice cream 16–19 °F | sorbet 10–14 °F
c0137: Pour the mix into the batch freezer and start the cycle
c0138: Add swirls, mix-ins or ripple in the last minute, if used
c0139: Draw the ice cream into a pre-chilled pan with a spade
c0140: Label the pan: flavor, production date, use-by date and batch — shelf life by food group is in the table at the bottom of this sheet
c0141: Weigh the pan and log yield / overrun (ice cream must weigh at least 4.5 lb per gallon, 21 CFR 135.110; gelato has no federal standard)
c0143: Harden the pan to 0 °F or below in the blast freezer (freezing cycle) — log reading: ____ °F
c0144: Move the pan to the storage freezer, 0 °F to −4 °F — log reading: ____ °F
c0145: Log the day's production: flavor, lb, batch, destination
c0146: Clean the batch freezer per the manufacturer: remove the dasher, scraper blades and door gasket, clean the cylinder in place, then sanitize
c0147: Clean, then sanitize production surfaces and utensils used (test strip)
c0148: SHELF LIFE GUIDE — adjust it to your product, equipment and supplier
c0151: House-made ice cream and sorbet in a covered pan
c0153: In the dipping cabinet quality drops within 3–5 days: rotate by flavor, not by the long freezer date
c0154: Pasteurized base mix, not yet batch-frozen
c0156: Never freeze the base: it separates and loses structure when thawed
c0157: Assembled ice cream cakes and semifreddo
c0159: Wrapped and boxed: they soak up freezer odors very easily
c0162: Freeze in single-use portions: never thaw and refreeze
c0165: Nut fat goes rancid without warning: always put the opening date on the jar
c0168: The clock starts at OPENING: write it on the container the same day
